name: Hassan Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Hassan. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can be as frank as you like. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at seven with a double-up call, that's two carers together, for a gentleman called Mr Alves who needs the hoist to get out of bed. I work for one of the big home care companies in the city, about four hundred of us, and I'm one of maybe twenty men. So I get a lot of the older men who'd rather not have a young woman washing them, which I understand. I do about eleven calls a day, mostly on the bus and on foot, and I'm usually home by seven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the old men's stories, honestly, Mr Alves worked on the docks for forty years and he still tells me how to tie a rope properly. The hard part is the fifteen-minute calls, when you've got someone to toilet and feed and there's no time to talk. And my back, after six years of hoists and bad beds. Some of the beds in these flats are lower than a sofa.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Just me, in a rented flat above a bakery on Mill Lane, so the mornings smell good at least. My dad runs a small tiling business and my uncle Karim is an electrician, and my mum asks me every Sunday when I'm getting married. I've got about three months of wages saved. I use one of those AI chat apps now and then, mostly the translation for Mr Alves when his Portuguese comes out, and once to write a letter to my landlord about the damp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said. There'll always be old people, and somebody has to look after them. At work the lads would joke that the robots aren't coming to do the hoist after all. Online I'd keep quiet, I don't argue with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think my job is fine, maybe better than fine, because the company is always short of carers. Every week the coordinator rings me begging for extra calls. Rent on Mill Lane goes up every year, but I've got overtime whenever I want it, so I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, really. I'd keep doing my eleven calls, take the extra Saturday shifts when they come, and keep putting a bit aside for a deposit. Maybe I'd use the translation app a bit more with Mr Alves, because it does help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed, to be honest. My back worries me more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your back worries you. What happens to your money if it gives out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the real risk, yes, because I'm paid by the call and there's no big sick pay. I've got about three months saved, so I could ride out a bad few weeks. After that I'd have to lean on my dad, and I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything routine in your job that a computer might take over even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company already sends the rota through an app, and I suppose it could get smarter at planning the routes. That would be nice, actually, if it stopped sending me from one end of the city to the other at lunchtime. It's the coordinator's job that changes, not mine.

say: There'll **always be old people**, and somebody has to look after them.
The lads at work would joke that **robots aren't coming** to do the hoist.
think: My job is **fine**, because the company is **always short** of carers.
The coordinator begs me for **extra calls** weekly, so overtime covers the rising rent.
do: Keep doing **eleven calls a day** and take the extra Saturday shifts.
Keep putting a bit aside each month towards a **flat deposit**.
Use the **translation app** more often with Mr Alves.
feel: **Relaxed**; his **back** worries him more than any computer.
S0.quote: There'll always be old people, and somebody has to look after them.
fieldNote: He reads **steady demand** for carers as real job security, and the overtime backs that up.
His one honest risk is **his back**, because pay is by the call with little sick pay.
He'd welcome **smarter routing**, which shows he's open to tools that are proven to help.

steps.text: Take the extra Saturday shifts the coordinator offers
Set aside part of each month's overtime for a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office jobs that change, not ours, and I'd say it kindly, because some of those coordinators are good people. With my friends I'd say this is why my dad always told me to learn something with your hands. I'd probably share one of those videos of a robot falling over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company would cut coordinators and let an app plan everything, and some days that would go wrong. My own hours would be safe for years. Nobody is building a robot for an old docker's hoist any time soon, but an app could time every call to the minute. Then those fifteen-minute calls get even tighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new app they bring in properly, not just the minimum, because the ones who learn it get the better rotas. I'd ask the trainer for the voice notes, so I can speak my care notes on the bus instead of typing them in someone's kitchen. Otherwise I'd keep going and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for the office staff, but fine for myself. It's like watching weather in another town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bianca, one of our coordinators, she's got two kids and she's the one who knows which clients get confused in the evenings. If an app does her job, I don't know where she goes, maybe back out on calls like us. She'd do it, but her knees aren't great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the calls might get tighter. What would you do if they did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the manager first, politely, with times written down. If it didn't change, I'd look at the other agency across the river, because they pay the same and everyone says they're less rushed. I don't like jumping, but I'd jump for that.

say: It's the **office jobs** that change, not ours, and some coordinators are good people.
My dad was right: **learn a trade** with your hands.
think: The company would **cut coordinators** and let an app plan the rotas.
My own hours stay **safe for years**, since no robot is near the hoist.
Calls timed to the minute would make **fifteen-minute calls** even tighter.
do: Learn the company's **new rota app** properly to get the better rotas.
Ask the trainer for **voice notes** so he can speak care notes on the bus.
feel: **Uneasy** for the office staff, but **fine** for himself.
S1.quote: Nobody is building a robot for an old docker's hoist any time soon, but an app could time every call to the minute.
fieldNote: He worries for **Bianca**, a coordinator with two kids, more than for himself.
Being **steady** for him means learning the app properly once the company makes it standard.
He'd only switch agencies if **rushed calls** got worse, and he'd raise it with the manager first.

steps.text: Learn the new rota app and voice notes properly
Keep his eleven daily calls and Saturday overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should calm down and look after their own, because that's what families are for. At the mosque and at my dad's table I'd say the government shouldn't hand out money for nothing, it should help people get a trade. Online I'd still stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 2028 doesn't scare me much. AI that thinks can't wash an old man, but robots in 2031 mean the company replaces me the minute they're cheaper. I'd be thirty-two, and they're a business, so I've got about five years and I'd be stupid to waste them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd talk to my uncle Karim about an electrician apprenticeship, evenings and weekends first, while I keep my care hours. I'd push my savings from three months to six by cutting the takeaways and the gym. Once AGI landed in 2028, I'd go to Karim full time if he'd have me, because the robots would still be three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan. I'd feel the clock, that's for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrician, if robots can do hands-on work too by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rewiring a hundred-year-old flat is a mess, every one is different, and people want a person they trust in their house. My uncle says he's crawled under floors no robot will see for years. Maybe I'm wrong, but it buys me more time than lifting people does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say when you told her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say good, finally a proper trade, and then she'd ask about getting married again. She's always thought care was women's work, though she'd never say it to my face. My dad would just nod and ask Karim how much I'd be paid.

say: Families should **look after their own** first, and people should calm down.
Government should help people **get a trade**, not hand out money for nothing.
think: Thinking AI in 2028 can't wash Mr Alves, but **robots in 2031** will replace me.
The company will buy robots the minute they're cheaper, so I have **five years**.
do: Start an **electrician apprenticeship** with his uncle Karim on evenings and weekends now.
Push savings from **three to six months** by dropping takeaways and the gym.
Move to **Karim's firm full time** once thinking AI lands in 2028.
feel: **Worried** but holding **a plan**, with the clock always in mind.
S2.quote: AI that thinks can't wash an old man, but robots in 2031 mean the company replaces me the minute they're cheaper.
fieldNote: He reads the **three-year gap** as a window to move, not a reprieve.
His plan leans on **family**: uncle Karim's trade, with his dad checking the pay.
He believes a **messy, varied trade** like old wiring buys more time than lifting people does.

steps.text: Start electrician training with uncle Karim on evenings and weekends
Raise savings from three to six months of rent
Drop takeaways and the gym membership
Join uncle Karim's firm full time once AGI lands

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so use it, don't moan about it. I'd tell the younger lads at work to get a second skill while they're still being paid. That's what my dad did when the factories closed, he learned tiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2031 for AGI and 2034 for robots puts me at thirty-five before my job really goes. That's enough time to do it properly, not in a panic. I could get a real qualification and still have most of my working life left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the evening course in electrical installation at the college on Ring Road next September, two nights a week, while doing my care calls. I'd save a bit every month for the exam fees and tools, maybe a hundred a month. Around 2031 I'd switch over to Karim's firm or apply to a bigger contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's a manageable kind. Like knowing a big exam is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two nights a week on top of eleven calls a day. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be hard, I won't lie, I'd be falling asleep on the bus. But I'm single, no kids, no one waiting for me at home except the smell of bread, so if I don't retrain now I never will. At thirty-two with a wife it would be much harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still worry about anyone at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older women carers, the ones in their fifties. They've done this thirty years and they're not going to college at night. I'd tell them to talk to the union or whoever helps, but I'm not really a union person myself.

say: There's **time, so use it**, instead of moaning about it.
Younger carers should get a **second skill** while they're still being paid.
think: Robots in **2034** put me at thirty-five before the job really goes.
That's enough to get a **real qualification** with most of my working life left.
do: Enrol on the **evening electrical course** at the Ring Road college next September.
Save about **100 a month** for exam fees and tools.
feel: **Uneasy** but manageable, like a **big exam** coming.
S3.quote: I'm single, no kids, no one waiting for me at home except the smell of bread, so if I don't retrain now I never will.
fieldNote: Five years of warning turns his plan from a **rush** into a **proper qualification**.
He sees being **single and childless** now as the reason to act early.
He worries for **older women carers** but keeps his distance from unions himself.

steps.text: Enrol on the evening electrical course at the college next September
Put 100 a month aside for exam fees and tools
Keep his care calls while studying two nights a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who says they had no warning wasn't listening. At work I'd say it with a smile, because it's a long way off. My friends would probably tease me for planning so far ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, robots in 2039 means I'd be forty, and that's a long way from now. In that time I might be married, maybe a supervisor, maybe something else. So it's on my mind, but not every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my care job for now and think about the nursing apprenticeship the hospital runs, because nurses do the thinking and the hands-on. Or the electrician course later, when I've saved more. In the first year I'd mostly save and ask around, I wouldn't rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small itch. Ten years is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mention nursing. Wouldn't thinking AI change that too, around 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Somebody still has to be responsible when a patient's care goes wrong, and I think that'll be a person for a long time. I'd be qualified by thirty-one and have a few years before anything bites. If I'm wrong, I'll have Karim's trade to fall back on, because he'll still be working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about the wedding, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's coming, just not this year. With ten years to plan I'd want to be settled in a proper job before I bring a wife into it. My dad married at thirty and he says it was the right age.

say: **Ten years** is plenty, and nobody can say they had no warning.
I'd say it at work **with a smile**, since it's a long way off.
think: Robots in **2039** put me at forty, a long way from now.
By then I could be **married**, a supervisor or in another trade, so it's not daily.
do: Keep his **care job** and look into the hospital's **nursing apprenticeship**.
Save more before deciding on the **electrician course** later.
Ask around for a year **before committing**, instead of rushing.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with a **small itch** about the future.
S4.quote: Somebody still has to be responsible when a patient's care goes wrong, and I think that'll be a person for a long time.
fieldNote: With a decade he **widens the options** to nursing as well as the electrical trade.
He keeps **Karim's trade** as a fallback, which shows how much family shapes his plans.
Marriage waits until he's **settled in work**, a traditional sum he takes from his dad.

steps.text: Keep his care calls with the same company
Ask the hospital about its nursing apprenticeship next year
Wait a year before choosing between nursing and electrics

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because five years to robots isn't long when you're paying rent and learning a trade at night. What would help is paid apprenticeships for people like me, a wage while you learn, not a handout. And some way to keep carers for the old men who'll never trust a machine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the old people's families. If families paid a bit more and visited a bit more, half these robots wouldn't be needed. I'd rather see a son wash his father than a machine do it.

headlineQuote: I'd rather see a son wash his father than a machine do it.
portrait: Hassan, 27, is one of few **male carers** at a big city agency, doing eleven calls a day.
He's single, rents a flat above a **bakery**, and has about **three months** saved.
He uses AI **now and then**, mostly translation for a client, and learns tools once they're proven.
He's calm about the plateau but sees robots as a **countdown** in the fast AGI picture.
His answer is a **trade through family**: an electrician apprenticeship with his uncle Karim, or nursing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because five years to robots is short while paying rent and learning at night.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** with a wage while you learn, not a handout.
Keeping human carers for old men who'll **never trust** a machine.
